Pregnancy

Enoxaparin in pregnancy: injections, safety and birth planning

Updated: November 14, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

If you have been sent home with enoxaparin injections, the first question to ask is why you need them. Preventing a blood clot and treating one that has already formed involve different doses, follow-up and birth plans. A demonstration with your own syringe and a written plan for the weeks around delivery can make the prescription easier to manage.

Find out what the prescription is meant to do

Enoxaparin belongs to a group of anticoagulants called low-molecular-weight heparins. It reduces the activity of clotting factors, particularly factor Xa. If you already have a deep vein thrombosis (DVT), the injection helps prevent it from growing and helps protect against further clots while your body gradually breaks it down. A clot that travels to the lungs can cause a pulmonary embolism (PE), which needs emergency care.

A prescription can also be preventive. Someone admitted to hospital with severely reduced mobility might receive injections for a short period. Someone who develops a DVT late in pregnancy may still need treatment months after the birth. Both may leave the pharmacy carrying similar syringes. Ask the prescriber to write down the indication, strength, amount per injection, frequency and date for review.

How the team decides who needs prevention

Tell your maternity team about previous clots, including when they happened and whether pregnancy, an oestrogen-containing medicine, surgery or prolonged immobility was involved. A close relative’s clot, a known clotting disorder and current medical problems can affect the assessment. Age is one consideration among several. Turning a particular age by itself does not establish that you need an anticoagulant.

Your risk can change between appointments. Contact the team if you are admitted to hospital, become unusually immobile or are struggling with persistent vomiting and dehydration. Birth also changes the balance, particularly after a caesarean, prolonged labour or heavy blood loss. The team will consider the risk of bleeding alongside the risk of a clot. Local guidance may differ on the combination of factors that warrants injections.

When pregnancy loss is the concern

After a miscarriage, it is reasonable to ask what an injection would change in a future pregnancy. Repeated losses have several possible causes. In appropriately diagnosed antiphospholipid syndrome (APS), a specialist may recommend low-dose aspirin together with heparin. This decision depends on the clinical and laboratory history. A single abnormal result or an unexplained loss does not establish that the combination will help.

Inherited thrombophilia is a separate question. In the ALIFE2 trial, heparin did not improve the chance of live birth in women with inherited thrombophilia and repeated pregnancy loss. Someone with the same diagnosis might still need clot prevention for her own health. Ask which outcome the prescriber is aiming to improve before starting treatment. If you use anticoagulation for a mechanical heart valve, contact your cardiology and maternity specialists promptly about pregnancy. Valve protection requires its own regimen and monitoring. Changing or missing treatment can be dangerous.

What is known about safety for you and the baby

Low-molecular-weight heparins do not pass through the placenta in clinically meaningful amounts. This is one reason maternity teams use them when an anticoagulant is needed. Available human data on enoxaparin are reassuring about major birth defects, although they cannot guarantee the outcome of an individual pregnancy. Untreated thrombosis also puts the pregnant person and the pregnancy at risk.

The principal risk for the person receiving enoxaparin is bleeding. Before the first dose, tell the prescriber about recent bleeding, kidney problems, previous low platelets or a past reaction called heparin-induced thrombocytopenia. Bring a list of prescriptions, non-prescription medicines and supplements. Aspirin or an anti-inflammatory painkiller such as ibuprofen can add to bleeding risk. If aspirin is already part of a specialist plan, check before changing it.

Learn with the syringe you will use at home

Ask a nurse, midwife or pharmacist to watch you practise with your own type of syringe. Check the strength and the amount you were told to inject. Some prefilled syringes contain precisely one prescribed dose. Other prescriptions need a measured amount from a graduated syringe. If the box or markings look different after a refill, have the pharmacy check them before the next injection is due.

Enoxaparin is usually injected into fatty tissue under the skin of the abdomen. Select the area your clinician demonstrated, away from the navel, bruises, scars or irritated skin, and rotate sites. For example, the Clexane instructions specify at least 5 cm from the navel. The Lovenox prefilled device normally contains an air bubble that should stay in the syringe. Ask for a demonstration if the prescribed amount is less than the contents. Leave a damaged, cloudy or visibly contaminated syringe unused and contact the pharmacy for a replacement.

Use the skin fold and needle angle shown for your product. Afterward, avoid rubbing the injection site. Put the used syringe directly into an approved sharps container and ask where to take the full container. If reaching the site or handling the syringe becomes difficult as pregnancy advances, arrange another demonstration or have a support person trained. Moving the injection to an unapproved site may change how the medicine is delivered.

Keep a record of doses and blood tests

Write down the actual time of each injection. Linking it to an ordinary routine can help, especially when different people sometimes give the dose. If you miss one, check your written instructions and contact the prescribing team if the next step is unclear. If you are unsure whether a dose went in, do not give yourself a second injection to make up for it. If you take too much, seek urgent advice even if you feel well.

How long an injection affects clotting depends on the dose, schedule and how well your kidneys clear the medicine. An estimate of peak activity cannot tell you when it is safe to have an epidural or another procedure. Your team may check your blood count, platelets and kidney function. A specialised anti-Xa measurement is useful in selected circumstances. Routine anti-Xa testing is generally unnecessary for most pregnant patients receiving standard treatment for a clot.

Recognise bleeding and symptoms of a new clot

A small bruise or brief soreness where you injected is common. Contact the maternity or prescribing team promptly for unusual bleeding, a spreading or painful skin reaction, repeated nosebleeds, blood in the urine or black, tarry stools. Vaginal bleeding in pregnancy warrants maternity advice. Heavy bleeding, feeling faint or collapsing calls for emergency care. Tell the team your last injection time and any other medicines that affect bleeding.

Get emergency help for sudden breathlessness, chest pain, coughing blood, collapse, a sudden severe headache or a new problem speaking, seeing or moving a limb. A swollen, painful leg, particularly on one side, needs urgent assessment. An injection lowers the risk of a clot but cannot exclude one. Swelling of the face or throat or difficulty breathing after an injection can also be an emergency.

Make a labour and anaesthesia plan before the due date

Ask the maternity and anaesthesia teams to record what to do if contractions begin, your waters break, bleeding starts or a planned induction changes date. If you think labour has started, call the maternity unit promptly, tell them when and how much you last injected, and follow their instructions before any further injection. The usual obstetric advice is to withhold further heparin when labour starts. If you have a mechanical valve, follow the individual specialist plan and get immediate advice.

An epidural or spinal injection too soon after anticoagulation carries a rare risk of bleeding around the spinal nerves. Common minimum waiting periods are 12 hours after some preventive regimens and 24 hours after treatment doses. The anaesthetist determines the interval for your actual dose, kidney function and procedure, including removal of an epidural catheter. These times are not a countdown for restarting at home. After spinal or epidural anaesthesia, new severe back pain, leg weakness or numbness, or a change in bladder or bowel control needs emergency assessment.

Before leaving the maternity unit

Ask for the first postpartum dose time in writing. It depends on bleeding, the birth, anaesthesia and your reason for taking anticoagulation. The risk of venous clots is particularly high just after birth. Some people need only a short preventive course and others need several weeks. With a confirmed pregnancy-associated DVT or PE, treatment usually continues through pregnancy and for at least six weeks after delivery, with at least three months of treatment in total. A late clot can mean continuing longer.

Low-molecular-weight heparin is generally compatible with breastfeeding. Before discharge, check who will supply the syringes, who will review any bleeding and who will decide the stop date. Keep the written plan with your maternity records. If an emergency or a new procedure takes you to a different hospital, show the team the medicine name, prescribed amount and time of the last injection.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Use the indication, bleeding risk, kidney function and maternity plan to interpret a prescription.

Keep miscarriage treatment for diagnosed APS distinct from venous clot prevention and treatment.

Follow instructions for the dispensed syringe and obtain individual timing advice before labour, procedures or dose changes.

How BeMama can help

BeMama explains the questions to discuss when enoxaparin is prescribed. Your maternity, prescribing and anaesthesia teams decide the dose, timing and monitoring.

When to seek help

Heavy bleeding, collapse, sudden breathlessness or chest pain, new weakness or difficulty speaking, or severe neurological symptoms after a spinal procedure need emergency assessment. For suspected labour, contact the maternity unit immediately with the time and amount of the last injection.

Evidence notes updated: November 14, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Check whether your injection is for clot prevention, treatment or a specialist condition.
  • A previous pregnancy loss alone does not establish a reason to start heparin.
  • Use the syringe and amount you were shown, and keep a record of each injection time.
  • Ask for individual instructions about labour, epidural timing and restarting after birth.
  • Heavy bleeding, sudden chest symptoms or new neurological symptoms require emergency care.

Frequently asked questions

How do I give an enoxaparin injection in pregnancy?

Have your team show you with the exact device you will use. Check the prescribed amount, alternate approved sites under the skin and dispose of the syringe in a sharps container. If you are uncertain about a bubble, the markings or a partial dose, ask before injecting.

Which side effects should I report?

Small local bruises are common. Report unusual bleeding, black stools, blood in urine or a spreading rash promptly. Heavy bleeding, sudden weakness, severe headache, chest pain, breathing difficulty or collapse needs emergency help.

Who needs enoxaparin while pregnant?

It can treat a clot or reduce the chance of one when your history and current circumstances indicate a significant risk. Some people with APS have a separate indication. The team considers your bleeding risk as well. A relative’s dose, your age alone or a history of miscarriage cannot determine your prescription.

Could the medicine harm my baby?

Enoxaparin does not cross the placenta in clinically meaningful amounts. Human data have not shown a clear rise in major birth defects. The team still weighs the risks of bleeding and of an untreated clot for you and the pregnancy.

What if I miss an injection or cannot remember whether I took it?

Look at your record, then follow the plan supplied with your prescription. If the timing is unclear, call your pharmacist or maternity team and explain when the last definite injection was. Avoid a double dose to compensate.

Can I still have an epidural?

Often you can, provided enough time has passed since the last injection and the anaesthetist considers it safe. Bring the exact amount and time to the assessment. The team can discuss alternative pain relief if labour advances before that interval has passed.

Will the injections end as soon as the baby is born?

The discharge plan sets the restart and stop dates. A short course of prevention after birth differs from treatment for an established clot, which may extend for several months. Tell the team if bleeding or a new procedure changes the plan.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
